Something I question about VtES is why the Crypt deck is random...
since it doesn't really need to be. If you need a vampire out, you just
play with 4-5 copies of it. However, this rule really puts a limit on
what a deck can do. And its a pain to shuffle 12 card decks. So...

What about a format where you chose the order of your Crypt? Would it

>Something I question about VtES is why the Crypt deck is random...
>since it doesn't really need to be. If you need a vampire out, you just
>play with 4-5 copies of it. However, this rule really puts a limit on
>what a deck can do. And its a pain to shuffle 12 card decks. So...

I don't see how it's a pain to shuffle 12 cards. Deal them out into
random piles, cut them, deal out again, table shuffle etc. It's not
very hard.

And it doesn't really put a limit on what a deck can do. It puts a
limit on what some decks can do (if they really want to force a vampire)
by giving them cluttered uncontrolled regions, but has absolutely no
bearing on other decks. So some decks get exactly the vampire they
want, and others don't. Some decks care about that, other decks don't.

That's not a "limit", that's a trade-off. You can build big libraries
that have lots of cards, or small libraries that are much tighter. That
doesn't limit either deck, but it's a trade off of what you get -
staying power vs efficiency, an empty library vs not drawing quite what
you want due to the joys of random probability.

Which such decks would you say are underpowered, at the moment? They
seem to be pretty balanced against decks that don't care much what their
crypt is, but this would significantly up their power, surely. Is that
warranted?

>What about a format where you chose the order of your Crypt? Would it
>open up more deckbuilding options? Would it break anything?

Break is a subjective term, particularly when it comes to vampires.
However, it does have some side effects.

1a) Do you *really* want Arika decks to only have to include 2 copies of
Arika, and not have any chance of choking (too many or too few),
so that it can bring Arika out, have a back-up, and have two
different vampires of its choice, every time?

1b) Same question, for a Stanislava Dominate-Protean deck. Woo, 2
Stanislavas, an Ingrid Rossler and an Illiana?

1c) Generally, these are very powerful decks, and one of the significant
balancing factors is that the deck can get screwed over by
forcing one vampire. Do we really want rid of this sort of
thing? The Eldest are Kohlo Tsunda with guaranteed Tsunda?
Matthias Spirit Marionette and a horde of weenies, guaranteed?

2) While it is certainly arguable that the Advancement rule is quite
weak at the moment (in the sense of being relatively hard to
pull off), this would significantly up its power by reducing the
opportunity cost very, very hard. As it stands, it seems likely
that the designers wanted it to be costly to merge a vampire -
you have to go to some effort to do it, in terms of bringing out
both vampires, or "wasting" master phase actions, library slots,
pool etc.

I'm not really sure I want a very speedy bring out of Helena,
followed by a merge on the next turn, followed by lots of
Kindred Coercions shutting down vote decks.

3) Talking of vote decks, Legacy of Pander is still a useful card, even
it its not so powerful state. One of the interesting features
of decks running it was trying to get it out at the start. They
want vampires with Presence, to push a vote against an earlier
popular Prince (say, Volker) who could stop it, even if they
bled to get the Edge. Only two small Pander have Presence -
Angela Decker and Lena Rowe. (Also Alfred, at 6/7, but he has a
title and is big.) So decks would sometimes run Caitiff with
Presence, or double up on vampires, or whatever, meaning that
things could sometimes go non-optimally. You might not get many
Pander to start with, or duplicate some of them, so the deck
doesn't just run away with itself. Now, Angela and Lena in the
first four vampires, no problem.

4) Minor niggle: The Stranger Humongous and Recruitment drop so far in
utility that they're pretty much wallpaper, and it's not like
they're overly played now.

5) It becomes relatively easy to include a throw-away vampire of a
"wrong" clan, to meet requirements. Want some vote push? Okay,
Rufina Soledad plus some Ventrue Headquarters in your deck.
This is particularly easy if the deck already uses Fortitude in
some way, but doesn't particularly need Ventrue much. Similar
scenarios are available for other set-ups. Mixed clan decks
have historically had potentially potent discipline
combinations, at the cost of not being able to rely on clan
toys. This changes that expectation radically. (Incidentally,
this could downgrade specials such Tatiana Stepanova's or Mata
Hari's.)

Dai wrote:
> What about a format where you chose the order of your Crypt? Would it
> open up more deckbuilding options? Would it break anything?

As James points out, it would likely be open to all sorts of abuse.
That being said, when testing out new decks in casual play, we aren't
in any way above stacking crypts (in the sense of "I'm trying out this
new deck--I'm gonna stack my crypt...") or building decks with illegal
crypts in the name of trying something out (Dave is well known for
showing up with 4 card crypts when he is trying something crazy that he
doesn't have all the cards for).

VTES is all about cost and effect. Crypt building is part of that. If
you want, say, to draw a particular vampire as he is perfect for your
crypt (i.e. effect), you have to include multiples on him in your crypt
(cost). The higher the likelyhood of drawing Vampire X from your crypt
(i.e. the more you put in) the higher the likelyhood of drawing nothing
*but* that vampire in your opening draw (which is the risk of using 5
or 6 of the same vampire). Cost and effect. Monkeying with this
increases the possible effect (i.e. getting a perfect crypt draw) while
reducing the cost (the risk of a bad crypt draw). Which isn't
necessarily a good thing.

Basically, if your group likes the idea of monkeying with stacked
crypts, try it out in casual play, and if you like it, keep doing it,
but it is unlikely to be something to become an offical variant or
whatever.

-Peter

Huh?!? You go on in this post to point a *bunch* of things that a deck
could do using this rule. I think I agree with the points you make
later on. Such a change would have too many insidious effects. It
would subvert play-balance in ways that would ultimately make the game
much less interesting or maybe downright boring depending on how few
playable deck archetypes remained after the ones that thrive under this
untested rule change choked out the rest.

However, one thing you _can't_ say is that the existing rule doesn't
put a limit on what a deck can do. It absolutely does - that's why
it's there. It's the same thing that the previous poster wanted to
do without it which exactly forms the core of the abuses that concerned
you. I think the point is that the game has been tested and balanced
with the existing rule in place so that existing cards and decks are
as well balanced as they can be in a CCG. You can't really go and
make a fundamental rule change from the set of rules the cards were
designed and playtested under and expect that balance to hold up.

In some ways, I appreciate the intent of the suggestion. I've always
kind of hated the extreme randomness effects of completely reordering
decks has on a CCG. It always drives me crazy that you can carefully
edit the number of cards in a library deck towards some important goal
and most games have your goal completely thwarted by having all of them
randomly shuffled to the last 30 cards in the deck, or the first 30,
or come up in pack in the middle, or some other weird configuration.
Unfortunately, for the most part, there's no real satisfactory
solution to that problem.

Fred

Sigh. Is it time for Fred loses the plot because someone doesn't define
what they're saying to the n-th degree again? I was hoping we could put
that off for a while longer. Oh well.

It's a balancing factor and a trade-off. If you want to treat that as a
limit, sure, knock yourself out. People can, and do, put together all
sorts of crazy-ass decks, with all sorts of cards, but everything has
its price in V:TES.

Only having 90 cards in your library is a "limit". 7 cards in your hand
is a "limit". Only having 30 pool is a "limit". Yet I would never
complain that only having 30 pool limits what a deck can do. It's just
how the game works. You don't have infinite pool, so that you have
different meaningful choices. You don't get to set your library order,
so you have different meaningful choices. You don't get to set your
crypt order, so you have meaningful choices.

Meaningful choices create a framework for strategy and differentiation.
Meaningful choices mean that the differences between an average player
and a strong player are magnified, because the strong player has another
meaningful choice to make. Does that "limit" the average player? Sure,
knock yourself out.

But you know, you work with the choices you're given. You want a deck
where you can bring out Arika, Queen Anne and Suhailah? You can build
it. People do build them. The choices you make affect your deck. The
choices I make affect mine. I can still build the Legacy of Pander deck
and make a strong setup for bringing out a Presence oriented vampire - I
can include duplicate vampires, I can include weenie Presence vampires
who will let me pass (but won't benefit from) the Legacy of Pander -
perhaps a copy of Lolita or Frederick the Weak to spice things up and
make my life a little bit easier in some ways, but in some ways a little
bit harder.

Only being able to play with cards you have a legal copy of is a
"limit", too. Grouping is a "limit". These are just basic axioms of
V:TES. They're a "limit" in much the same way that the law of gravity
is a "limit" on your behaviour.

>You go on in this post to point a *bunch* of things that a deck
>could do using this rule.

Things that could be *guaranteed*, not things that can't be done or
tried now.

You can still those things using the present rules set, but you have a
meaningful choice to make - do I use library slots for Gift of
Experience, do I use different technology in my deck to push a vote, do
I include Recruitment in my deck, do I allow the probability of deck
shuffling to be the over-riding factor in the success of getting the
vampires I want.

You want a Ventrue out to play the HQ? Well, you can do that. Or you
can go for Mata Hari, to nullify the need for one. Or you can include
Clan Impersonation. Or you can do a whole heap of other things. Is
that a limit? Go ahead, if you must. It's a cost, it's a
consideration, it's a choice for a deck-builder to make. They get it
right, or maybe they get it wrong. They don't get it for free, because
we generally want a game where the challenge differentiates players.

These are balancing factors. If you want to call those limits, fine. I
don't call clan requirements "limits", but I'll be expecting you to call
them that in the future. I don't call blood costs "limits", but sure,
you go ahead and do that.

>However, one thing you _can't_ say is that the existing rule doesn't
>put a limit on what a deck can do.

If you read beyond the sentence you quoted, you'd see a fuller and more
detailed explanation.

That's not a "limit", that's a trade-off. You can build big
libraries that have lots of cards, or small libraries that are
much tighter. That doesn't limit either deck, but it's a trade
off of what you get - staying power vs efficiency, an empty
library vs not drawing quite what you want due to the joys of
random probability.

It's a trade off chosen by the designers to create meaningful strategy,
just like not being able to have an infinite number of tanks, soldiers
and resources in a hex-map wargame creates meaningful strategy, or
having to choose between being a warrior or a mage in Dungeons and
Dragons gives meaningful differentiation between players. You get to
decide whether the costs exceed the benefit, whether you can work with
the costs, whether it will suit your playstyle.

It's a difference of intentionality, and the framework created. The
rules create the game, rather than limiting it. In some absolutist
sense, they limit everything by not being some other bunch of rules, but
they're not regarded as limits by and large because without them the
game just wouldn't be the game. They facilitate the game rather than
stifling it - assuming they're well executed.

The fact that the rules for V:TES aren't the same as the rules for Magic
is a "limit", and the fact that V:TES has a randomized crypt is a
"limit", and the fact that you have 12 vampires rather than 8 or 2 is a
"limit". The fact that my vampires need disciplines to play disciplined
cards is a "limit" - it stops me making some decks!

Everything in CCGs limits everything, everything in every game is a
limit, in this narrow absolutist sense. If you really, really, really
want to go down this road, the fact that LSJ won't print every card
we've ever suggested is a limit. The fact that I can't make up my own
vampires for sanctioned tournament play is a limit. The fact that there
isn't an OBE THA FOR PRE OBF vampire for 4 pool is a limit.

The horror of the limits. Oh, the horror. How I weep for the unborn
decks, stifled in the womb of creativity by the limits forced upon us.
But no, that's just the game, and how the game is designed and
developed.

I was just saying the comment above denies the exact point you later
affirmed: that the randomness of deck ordering indeed does limit what
a deck can do. When you complained that the proposal would allow an
Arika deck to get by with only two copies of Arika and still allow it to
be certain of drawing Arika, the problem is exactly that a limitation
caused by deck randomness would be circumvented. It's one and same
issue and it needs to be understood that way in order to understand
why the deck order has to be random.

At least, I _hope_ his comment about shuffling the deck being a pain
was thrown in as a joke...

>>You go on in this post to point a *bunch* of things that a deck
>>could do using this rule.

But the guarantee is realistically the whole point. Sure, I can play
with two copies of my key vampire. It's legal. I'll just lose
shitlessly a bunch of games I don't draw him/her/it and that will
make the memories of playing the deck very painful. Not many people
like playing with pain so they stop doing it. In the real, practical
world, randomness is clearly a limitation. It may not be as much of
one as if there was something written in the rules, people may choose
to ignore it and lose (much more commonly, we all push the edges of
good judgment in order to play something we like) but so what?
The motivation of deckbuilding is ultimately to build a deck that
wins. So your protests about the distinction between an absolute
vs. a practical limit are pretty much beside the point. I guess I
was assuming the guy wanted to order his crypt to get around the
practical limits or else I wouldn't see what the point would be.

> It's a trade off chosen by the designers to create meaningful strategy,
> just like not being able to have an infinite number of tanks, soldiers
> and resources in a hex-map wargame creates meaningful strategy, or
> having to choose between being a warrior or a mage in Dungeons and
> Dragons gives meaningful differentiation between players. You get to
> decide whether the costs exceed the benefit, whether you can work with
> the costs, whether it will suit your playstyle.

I understand all that. I appreciate that it's left to judgment
to decide how many copies of Arika I have to thrown in the deck to
balance the chances of not drawing her against the ability to draw
other, less crucial vampires. I just think making that distinction
in that context is beside the point. Random deck ordering is not the
only way a CCG could have been designed. Richard Garfield could have
designated the crypt to be a player-ordered pile of vampires and it
would have worked just fine as a game. It wouldn't have allowed
players to test their judgment about exactly how many copies of a
vampire they should use to make their deck work best. But it would
have allowed more leeway for focusing decks toward one strategy or
another and I think I might have liked the results better, especially
given that crypt deck ordering wouldn't have to be this horribly
capricious element to the game.

If there's any point to a person proposing to allow player-ordered
crypt decks, it's to circumvent the practical limit. Noting that
such randomness introduces a strategic element to the game is
meaningless at this point. It might be meaningful if we were all
sitting around designing a game from scratch but we're not. We're
talking about a real game with real cards that have already been
designed to the existing framework. And that is the relevant reason
why changing course at this point - even if just to the extent of
proposing an optional rule - is a proposal that's untenable.

> Everything in CCGs limits everything, everything in every game is a
> limit, in this narrow absolutist sense. If you really, really, really
> want to go down this road, the fact that LSJ won't print every card
> we've ever suggested is a limit. The fact that I can't make up my own
> vampires for sanctioned tournament play is a limit. The fact that there
> isn't an OBE THA FOR PRE OBF vampire for 4 pool is a limit.
>
> The horror of the limits. Oh, the horror.

Limits have their uses, as you note. And they have drawbacks. The fact
that you can't just make up vampires limits creativity in deckbuilding but
obviously it's a limit that needs to exist. On the other hand, there
is clearly an incentive to do away with it, at least to some degree. I
seem to recall a variant called "Create-A-Clan" that's been played in a
number of venues where large numbers of players gather. So apparently
the issue of limiting people to printed vampires isn't quite the slam
dunk you make it out to be. People like to discuss things like that.
Which is what the guy who started the thread was doing.

Fred

Heh, two days from now we'll play an unsanctioned tournament

I previously asked for input on what I called "Stacking the deck", a
format I believe I've stolen from this very newsgroup, and hopefully
modified somewhat.

Crypt: As usual.

Library: 60 - 90 cards.

Pregame:
Split library in three parts. A part must have at
least zero cards.
Designate each part starting deck, midgame deck and
endgame deck.
Shuffle each deck separately and place them in order.

Game:
Each player starts with their starting deck, which
for all purposes is considered their ENTIRE deck.
When first player is ousted starting deck is
discarded, all of it, including your hand.
Each player now plays their midgame deck. Same rules.
Second player ousted and it's time for the endgame
decks. Finish the game with the endgame decks.

There is certainly a number of BAD things that can occur if you do
this, but at least library-cards offer counters to other library
cards. It's equal for everyone, even though I can see some decktypes
gaining from this format. And - it's an unsanctioned tournament, for
fun :)

This is the format we have announced. Maybe starting and midgame decks
should have beem "removed from game" rather than "discarded". I don't
know.

"Chess" vs. "CCGs" is the very definition of the term "false dichotomy".
Sure, I understand that randomness, in some form, is a good thing.
Plus there are a number of random factors in the game having nothing
to do with deck ordering, like metagame matchups and even the
personalities of your various opponents which work well with or grate
on you (and vica versa), affect your abilities to work deals of
mutual benefit.

(For that matter a "random" factor in chess could be considered the
quality and play style of the opponent you draw. That's pretty
meager, but there it is.)

Anyway, I didn't mean to suggest anything of the sort like "randomness
is bad". But I wonder if people always apprectiate the degree and
importance of randomness in deck ordering. I don't think you'd
have turn the game into chess in order to back the randomness
down a bit. You could do a number of different things, like allow
players to draw their opening hand and shuffle the rest of the
cards. You could do something like Sten's "beginning game", "mid-
game", and "late game" decks (albeit I'm not sure I'd cause the
changeover to happen the same way but you get the point). There's
all sorts of mitigating rules you could create to address this
problem. You don't have to make decks be utterly random, from
card #1 to card #X (where X is the deck size). It just happened
that way because it it's the easiest and conceptually most
comprehensible thing you can do with a deck of cards. But it
really causes problems in CCGs.

to address this problem - although in Magic, some of them wound up
getting banned later because they had such an enormous effect on
strategy. The whole point of cards like Magic of the Smith, Sibyl's
Tongue, Fortschritt Library, and Muricia's Call is to address the
fact that cards may not come up in the right order, so here are
things that give you some ability to work around the problems
caused. They're kind of small mitigations of a huge issue, but
the fact that they exist at all says something.

Mulligans exist in several CCGs to address the issue (but only in the
"opening hand" sense).

But, yes, other options exist (and, indeed, an uncountable number of
them, probably).

For instance:

Have a player's library be "open" to him (but not to other players).
That way, you know exactly what's coming up and when (until you're
forced to reshuffle, of course -- but most of the "shuffle afterwards"
could then just be dropped, since they presuppose a closed library --
only the insertion of cards into the library would have to be "insert
at a random position in the library")

Or you could use a card holder to hold the queue of the top N cards of
the library, so those cards are visible to the owner. When you draw,
you draw the "top" card from the holder, slide the others over and turn
the next card form the library into the bottom slot of the holder.

Neither of which adjust the random arrangement of the deck, but they do
reduce the negative impact of it on play (so you can plan on the cards
you'll draw, rather than praying to top deck what you need).

Same for Crypt, naturally.

> You don't have to make decks be utterly random, from
> card #1 to card #X (where X is the deck size). It just happened
> that way because it it's the easiest and conceptually most
> comprehensible thing you can do with a deck of cards. But it

> really causes problems in TCGs.

Where "problems" is subjective (as per other places in this thread),
perhaps.

I think of it more as simply an aspect of card games. All card games.
An aspect that can be exploited (meaning simply taking into account) by
the rules (and, consequently, by saavy players) in any card game (where
"rules" includes card text for card games with rules-text-on-cards
logistics, like most TCGs). Whether by mulligan rules, deck striping
rules (like the separation of library and crypt in VTES, or
early-library/late-library separations in some house rules), deck
mining rules (like Magic of the Smith), &c.

you're just using tokens (possible hidden tokens, but tokens
nonetheless) -- as in Lord of the Rings, the Confrontation, which uses
a "deck" of 9 "cards" which the player "draws" all of into his hand of
9 and plays one at a time until his hand is exhausted, at which point
he draws them all back into his hand.

another. Did you think anything that qualifies as a strategy
element was always equally enjoyable as every other one? Wouldn't

> early game, mid game and late game strategy built in.

The clause, "to a very great extent" was intended to account for such
things. I realize the game contains things that lessen the impact.
I don't think it's lessened all that much, however. Your examples are
very specific deck archetypes. The vast majority of decks, including
many top tier decks, do little or nothing except to the extent that
they're built to optimize card flow.

>> This limits the kind of cards the designers can reasonably
>> bother designing and it limits the effectiveness of the ones they
>> do design.
>
> I think you're wrong there. The design team introduced Convictions in the most recent set and wanted to include a mechanism that
> allows players to always be able to get Convictions, despite shuffling. No problem.

Well, except that Convictions are a huge pain in the ass for exactly this
reason. And possibly imbued may be unbalancingly overpowered, depending
on who you ask. I agree that here's an example of a card designed to
specifically mitigate this problem. That doesn't mean the central design
of the game doesn't limit how cards can be designed, though. For instance,
if a designer wanted to create a card that allowed a balanced, moderate
advantage to a vampire deck that only made a difference at the beginning
of the game, it would be difficult to do. Due to the chance that it wouldn't
be drawn until too late, it would be impossible to balance without
increasing its advantage from moderate to high. I suppose he could invent
another new card type like Convictions that somehow guranteed (or made it
highly likely) that you could draw and use it early. But then he'd have
to add more rules to the game which I consider to be a bad thing. (More
rules -> more complexity -> harder to teach to newer players and keep track
of all the minutia and corner cases yourself.)

If your point is to say that anything is possible, I suppose that's true.
Still, the central design of the game makes certain things a lot harder
to do than others.

Fred

lessen it. I hadn't considered it but I suppose V:tES's striped

we don't have to draw away at our library decks to find vampires
before we can do anything. Being mana starved and mana-geysered
were two of the stupidest ways to lose a (Magic) game that I've
ever encountered as long as I've played games.

> Card games all have this aspect, by nature.

OK, I see what you're getting at. If you have cards in a pile, they
have to get piled by some means. The two extremes appear to be human
ordering and random 1-to-X shuffling. What I meant when I asked
if the "aspect" has to exist in every game is whether the 1-to-X
random shuffle extreme needs to always be the way to go. Choose
your opening hand, making one deck out of multiple decks intended
for different periods of the game (Sten's beginning, middle, and
end game decks), and all sorts of different rules can bring on
a something-in-between effect.

One amusing possibility: allow both (or all, in a multiplayer game)
to totally order their cards before the start - but then allow
cards in the game that permit players to alter other players decks
to some extent. If you did it right, there could be some very
interesting strategy trade-offs. For instance, the alternative
to cards that allowed a player to mess with their opponents decks
would be others that advanced their position towards winning. So
how many cards should you use of each type? I suspect the result
would be a bit of a matrix game and have a very random feel about
it - even though nary a card was ever shuffled (contrary to your
comment).

Even if you do shuffle, how important does it always have to be?

Fred
